name: Catherine Booth
title: Catherine Booth: a faith that spoke up and saw poverty
description: Cofounder of The Salvation Army, Catherine Booth brought together preaching, writing, and concern for the living conditions of working people.

sections.heading: A voice at the birth of a movement
paragraphs: Catherine Mumford was born in Derbyshire in 1829, into a family connected with Methodism. Her education at home included strong religious training. As Catherine Booth, she took part in founding and developing the movement that would become The Salvation Army.

From 1860 on she preached in public. She also wrote about the Christian life and defended the participation of women in proclaiming the gospel. Her intellectual and ministry contribution was part of the movement’s identity, together with the work of William Booth and many coworkers.

sections.heading: The gospel in the streets of London
paragraphs: The mission that began in London in 1865 sought to reach poor people and those left on the margins of church life. Its meetings were held in all kinds of places. In 1878 it took the name The Salvation Army, with its own organization and language.

Catherine supported social reforms, among them better conditions for women workers in London. She died in 1890. The Salvation Army’s heritage centre presents an account of her legacy that highlights both her preaching and her concern for people’s material lives.

reflection: In 1 John 3:16–18, love is recognized by a willingness to share and to act in the face of need. This teaching helps us examine our priorities: proclaiming Christ goes together with a life that takes seriously the hunger, exploitation, and neglect it finds around it.

Booth’s life also invites us to recognize the work of women who teach, write, and sustain communities. Differences among churches about ministry roles call for studying the relevant passages. That conversation can be held with respect, gratitude for service, and a willingness to listen.
review_note: Her historical position on women’s ministry is described without presenting it as a doctrinal agreement among all churches. Institutional figures are not carried over into the present.
source_labels: The Salvation Army, International Heritage Centre. “Catherine Booth.”
